raw_case_text:
The source patient was a 28-weeks' pregnant, 30-year-old woman of Kenyan origin who resided in France; she had visited Kenya and returned to France on June 1, 2001. On June 21, she was admitted to the gynecology-obstetrics emergency room at a greater Paris area hospital with fever and malaise. Blood sampling and thin and thick blood smears were performed by the nurse. The source patient's level of parasitemia was estimated at 0.05 per 100 erythrocytes, and oral quinine was initiated. The physician who interviewed the nurse after the needlestick injury verified that the source patient was HIV- and HCV-antibody negative and that the nurse was immunized against HBV. On June 23, although the results of her test for Plasmodium were negative, she was transferred to another tertiary care center where IV quinine was administered for nausea and vomiting, and she could be monitored more closely. She recovered fully and was discharged on June 27. Unfortunately, all blood samples or smears from the source patient had been discarded by the time the injured nurse became ill.
P. falciparum is a bloodborne pathogen, and malaria is a well-documented complication of transfusion. Malaria has also been diagnosed after intravenous drug use (,) and breaches in infection control procedures (-), as well as occupational exposures (-). Occupational P. falciparum infection after a needlestick injury may be rare; however, such an injury can be potentially severe in nonimmune healthcare workers in countries where malaria is not endemic, especially if the occupationally infected person is pregnant. This situation may also become more common as malaria spreads and as increasing international travel brings potential source patients to hospitals in malaria-endemic countries.
HBV, HCV, and HIV are the pathogens most often transmitted in documented cases of occupational infection following needlestick injuries in industrialized countries. Testing for infection by these pathogens does not include all the possible infections that can result from occupational exposure (,,). Although conducting a thorough investigation of the circumstances surrounding any needlestick injury is a challenge in the daily clinical setting, an investigation should always be carried out. As in this case-patient, the treatment of occupational P. falciparum infection may be delayed because physicians do not immediately consider malaria as a possible diagnosis. Furthermore, healthcare workers with neurologic symptoms caused by P. falciparum malaria may be too ill to tell the treating physician about their occupational exposure. Such infections must be diagnosed promptly as they are potentially lethal, and presumptive treatment is readily available and well tolerated. Clinicians managing healthcare or laboratory workers with a febrile illness or in a postexposure setting should consider the probability of occupational P. falciparum malaria.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old pregnant female presenting at 28 weeks' gestation with fever and malaise following recent travel to Kenya.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 30-year-old pregnant female at 28 weeks' gestation of Kenyan origin residing in France returned from Kenya on June 1, 2001. On June 21, she presented to an obstetric emergency department with acute fever and malaise. Blood smears were drawn (during which a treating nurse sustained a needlestick injury). Oral antimalarial therapy was started. On June 23, due to severe nausea and persistent vomiting precluding oral medication, she was transferred to a tertiary center for parenteral therapy and closer fetal-maternal surveillance.
subjective.past_medical_history: 28 weeks' gestation (gravida). Kenyan origin, residing in France. Travel to Kenya returning June 1, 2001. Baseline post-exposure contact serologies: HIV antibody negative, hepatitis C virus antibody negative.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, malaise, nausea, and vomiting. Negative for vaginal bleeding, rupture of membranes, uterine contractions, or dysuria. Medications: oral quinine initiated. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Pregnant female at 28 weeks' gestation. Febrile on presentation, nauseated. Vital signs stable. Obstetric examination confirmed reassuring fetal status; systemic physical examination otherwise unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline hematology and biochemistry. Thin and thick blood smears performed. Negative maternal HIV and HCV serologies.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in pregnancy (28 weeks' gestation) complicated by hyperemesis/intolerance of oral medication. (Source patient for an accidental needlestick transmission to a treating nurse).
Diagnostic confirmation: Initial blood smears demonstrating Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia of 0.05 per 100 erythrocytes (0.05%); repeat blood smears upon transfer were negative for circulating parasites. HIV and HCV antibodies confirmed negative.
Treatment & Outcome: Managed with oral quinine, switched to intravenous quinine upon transfer due to persistent vomiting. Monitored with serial fetal-maternal assessments. Experienced full symptom resolution, completed therapy, and was discharged in stable condition on June 27.
